Subject: Quick question on what Redwood keeps by default for interactive sessions

Hi Aisha —

We're wrapping up our security checklist for Redwood's evaluation. One area that's come up is the exact storage behavior for "interactive API sessions" when our users type messages into a product that calls your text-generation endpoint. Can you confirm the default behavior (without any customer opt-in):

- Are raw request payloads (user prompts) kept? If so, for how long?
- Are model outputs stored separately from requests? Retention for outputs?
- If tokens are streamed back to the client, are those intermediate fragments retained, or only the final response?
- Any differences between short-lived sessions vs. pinned conversation histories?

I've attached BrightBank_Security_Checklist.pdf with the exact checklist items — happy to mark the relevant lines if helpful.

Thanks,

Hi Emily —

Thanks for sending this over and for the checklist. Short answers up front, then I'll loop in Karthik and Kim for the exact policy notes you can include in your security package.

- Raw request payloads (user prompts): retained by default for 30 days. They are used for telemetry, billing reconciliation, and quality monitoring unless the customer enables a stricter opt-out.
- Model outputs: retained by default for 90 days. Outputs are stored as part of the session record and accessible by the customer through the Console until they expire.
- Streaming fragments: intermediate streamed token fragments are not persisted as separate objects by default; only the assembled final response is stored. If the customer uses server-side streaming capture for analytics, we surface that in the Console and tag it as ephemeral unless they opt to persist.
- Pinned conversation histories: anything a customer explicitly pins or exports (e.g., conversation exports, embeddings/indexes) is moved to a separate storage class and follows the customer's retention config or enterprise contract (can be indefinite by request).

I'll ask Karthik to provide the technical nuance (KV cache, indexing, embeddings) and Kim to confirm deletion/erasure steps for a full audit trail.

Best,

Emily —

Filling in the technical detail Aisha promised. Below are the default retention behaviors and some clarifying definitions we use internally (and that you can cite in your checklist).

Definitions:
- "Request (prompt)": the JSON payload sent by the customer containing user text, metadata (user_id, session_id if provided), and options.
- "Response (output)": the model's final assembled completion object (the thing returned by the API as the final response).
- "Stream fragment": intermediate token batches emitted during streaming.
- "Derived artifact": embeddings, reranker scores, indices, or cached KV artifacts created by the system or customer tools.

Default retention (hosted Redwood API, out-of-the-box):
- Requests (prompts): retained for 30 days. After 30 days requests are deleted from our active telemetry store; tombstone entries remain in audit logs for up to an additional 30 days for operational tracing before full purge (so total timeline for forensic traces can be up to ~60 days).
- Responses (model outputs): retained for 90 days in the session store. The reason for the longer output retention is to support replay, debugging, and conversation continuity features customers use in the Console.
- Stream fragments: by default we do not persist stream fragments as first-class objects; they are reconstructed into the final response and stored only as the final response. Exception: if the customer opts into detailed streaming analytics, fragments are written to a short-lived analytics bucket with a default TTL of 7 days.
- KV cache and runtime-only caches: these are ephemeral in-memory caches on the serving nodes and are not persisted to long-term storage. Crash recovery snapshots may be kept for a maximum of 7 days and are rotated.
- Derived artifacts: embeddings and indices are stored in a separate long-term store. Retention is configurable; without explicit customer configuration derived artifacts are not automatically purged and must be removed via Console or API.

Access and deletion paths:
- Customers can delete individual session records or request full-account erasure through the Console (Workspace > Security > Data & erasure). API-based erasure is available via the support endpoint (see link below) and requires an authenticated support ticket for complete removal of derived artifacts and audit traces.
- Programmatic erase: POST https://redwood.example.com/support/erase-request (support-assisted). For enterprise Private deployments we provide a runbook and direct KMS key rotation to remove access to archived objects.

One more note on privacy modes: customers can enable a "no-retain" mode for requests and outputs which reduces default retention to 0 days for prompts and 7 days for outputs (used by regulated pilots). That must be enabled per-workspace and is visible in the Console.

Attaching a small retention-matrix for quick reference. Happy to convert this into a one-page statement for your security team.

-Karthik
Director, Applied ML & Inference Policies

Emily —

Confirming what Karthik laid out and adding the practical steps BrightBank will want in an audit package:

1) Exportable evidence: we can provide a signed CSV export that lists session IDs, timestamps, retention expiration dates, and deletion hashes for any retention window. That export is generated via the Console audit panel.
2) Erasure confirmation: when BrightBank requests account erasure we provide a ticketed confirmation that lists which buckets/records were purged and the time of purge. For Hosted customers this includes the telemetry store, session store, and any analytics buckets (where applicable).
3) Derivative cleanup: to fully remove derived artifacts (embeddings, indexes), customers should submit an erase request and state whether they want derived artifacts purged — by default those are not auto-deleted unless requested.

I'll also include a short paragraph you can drop into your checklist: "By default Redwood retains user prompts for 30 days and model outputs for 90 days. Intermediate streaming tokens are not persisted unless analytics are enabled. Derived artifacts (embeddings, indices) are stored separately and require explicit deletion. Customers may opt into stricter no-retention modes or request full erasure via support."

If you'd like, we can schedule a 30-minute call with our security engineering team to walk through audit evidence and run a deletion request demo.

Thanks —
Kimberly Park
